newsitem.title: USA: Commerce corrects Feb U.S. trade deficit.
newsitem.headline: Commerce corrects Feb U.S. trade deficit.

text.p: The Commerce Department said Thursday the correct U.S. trade deficit for February was $10.4 billion instead of $11.59 billion as it reported earlier in the day.

The Commerce Department said "reporting errors" at several ports of entry had led to $1.1 billion of crude petroleum imports from prior periods being incorrectly shown as arriving in February. As a result, the entire monthly trade deficit figure was overstated.

A news service reported a possible error in the trade data late in the morning but it took several hours for the Commerce Department to investigate and issue its correction. Department officials would only say they were checking the numbers.
Late in the day, a prepared statement was released.

"As a result of data reporting errors at several ports of entry in the April 17 U.S. Commerce Department report on international trade ... an entry of approximately $1.1 billion for imports of crude petroleum from prior periods was incorrectly assigned to February 1997," Commerce spokeswoman Jane Callen said.

"Correcting this mis-reporting shows that the February level of crude petroleum imports as well as the total trade deficit, without seasonal adjustment, should have been $1.1 billion lower than reported," she said.
"Seasonally adjusted, the total trade deficit should be $1.2 billion lower than reported, or $10.4 billion," Callen said.
Economist Lawrence Chimerine of the Economic Strategy Institute said he had never seen such a huge correction made by a government agency on its own statistics on the day it issued them.

"Monthly numbers are erratic... but a billion dollars is not an insignificant amount," Chimerine said, adding it means that first-quarter economic growth likely will be stronger than would have been the case if there truly had been a $1.1 billion higher bill for oil imports.
